lots.title: VINTAGE ENAMEL TASMANIAN DAILY...
lots.findings: Blue and white vitreous enamel sign 'LEADING NEWSPAPER. THE DAILY TELEGRAPH. TASMANIA.' with 'MADE IN ENGLAND' at lower right. This is the Launceston Daily Telegraph, which ceased in 1928, so the sign is pre-1928 local Tasmanian advertising. Genuine enamel construction (rusted iron reverse with white enamel back coat).
lots.condition: Large enamel loss and rust to top right corner with a jagged edge, chips at fixing holes and edges, reverse heavily rusted. Face otherwise bright and glossy.
lots.identification: Single-sided vitreous enamel advertising strip sign, white sans-serif letters on cobalt blue: 'LEADING NEWSPAPER. / THE DAILY TELEGRAPH. / TASMANIA.' with 'MADE IN ENGLAND' small at lower right. 15 x 53 cm (catalogue). The Daily Telegraph was the Launceston daily paper (1883 to 1928, when it merged into The Examiner), so the sign predates 1928, probably 1900s to 1920s. Condition: top right corner has a large chunk missing or torn away with rust along the broken edge (the plate outline steps down there, so this is metal loss, not just chipping); small chips and rust at the fixing holes along top and bottom edges and at the corners; face enamel otherwise bright with good gloss and little fading. Back (photo 4) is rusted with green/grey counter-enamel and white enamel drips, consistent with genuine period enamel, not a modern reproduction (reproductions are usually printed tin or have clean backs).

lots.title: 3 BROAD ARROW STAMPED CONVICT ...
lots.findings: Three handmade sandstock bricks with finger-drawn marks: one incised with what looks like 'EAD' (or similar letters), one with a broad arrow (Government) mark, one with a 'WMVM'-style zigzag mark. Catalogue provenance: ex Alanvale, Newnham (Launceston). Only one brick clearly shows a broad arrow; the others carry other convict or maker marks.
lots.condition: Weathered, chipped edges and corners, mortar residue; one brick has a cracked surface.
lots.identification: Three handmade soft red clay bricks (not 'items' of metal: the catalogue lot is '3 BROAD ARROW STAMPED CONVICT BRICKS - EX-ALANVALE NEWNHAM', i.e. bricks recovered from Alanvale, Newnham, Launceston). Each has marks hand-incised into the wet clay before firing (drawn with a finger or stick, not a stamped frog): brick 1 (larger, paler, mortar on one edge) reads roughly 'L ^ D' with a broad arrow between letters; brick 2 has a single vertical stroke beside a large broad arrow; brick 3 reads roughly 'W ^ W' (or W ^ M) with a broad arrow in the middle. Bricks 2 and 3 also show deep finger/thumb impressions at the corners, the classic sign of hand moulding seen on Tasmanian convict-made bricks. These are consistent with genuine colonial (convict-era, c.1820s-1850s) Van Diemen's Land government bricks: broad arrow plus moulder's/gang initials scratched by hand is the typical Tasmanian convict pattern; later government issue used stamped marks in a frog, not hand scratching. Provenance (Alanvale) cannot be verified from photos. Bulky-ish and heavy (3 bricks, perhaps 9-10 kg).

Wall plate with 4 bolt holes, U-shaped hanging bracket, pivoting yoke with acorn finial, swinging pull arm for a rope, iron clapper tied with twine. Black painted finish, light rust at pivots. Pattern matches the common US farm-bell format (C.S. Bell / Hillsboro style) and the many later reproductions. Catalogue: estimate A$150-250; current bid A$220 at 10 Nov. Google Lens on photo 1: closest matches are modern 'antique style' cast iron school/dinner bells, eg The Renmy Store 'Large Cast Iron School Dinner Bell' 51 cm H x 38 cm W, 8.7 kg, A$239.95 new (same wall plate, U bracket, yoke, acorn finial and rope arm, though the lot's plate has 4 holes and a chamfered top). The clean casting, absence of any foundry name or 'No.' size mark and the twine-tied clapper point to a 20th/21st century reproduction rather than a 19th century C.S. Bell, Crystal Metal or similar US foundry bell (those carry cast names, size numbers and 1886 patent dates on the yoke). Estimated weight 8-12 kg.
